claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys can provide ultrahigh mechanical strength for high-temperature applications.
Refractory high-entropy alloys possess high thermal stability and resistance to softening at elevated temperatures.
A surface or interface engineering treatment can form an in situ nanolayered lubricious coating on a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Layered boron nitride or a stabilized MoS2-like phase is suitable as the proposed nanolayered tribolayer.
The proposed material is intended to operate through temperature fluctuations extending from cryogenic temperatures to above 1000 °C in oxidative environments.
The engineered tribolayer will remain continuous and thermally stable at the operating surface.
A surface tribolayer decouples lubrication from the load-bearing function of the refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix.
The inherent layered structure of the tribolayer produces low friction at elevated temperatures.
The nanolayered tribolayer minimizes wear without compromising the mechanical integrity of the underlying alloy.
The coated material will have a significantly lower coefficient of friction across a broad temperature range than the untreated alloy.
The coated material will have significantly lower wear rates across a broad temperature range than the untreated alloy.
The coated material will retain mechanical strength comparable to or slightly greater than that of the uncoated alloy.
The proposed composite will outperform conventional systems that use separate lubricating phases.
Conventional MoS2- or graphite-based lubricating agents lose lubrication efficiency at high temperatures.
Integrating conventional lubricating agents into a material tends to compromise its mechanical strength.
Temperature can increase friction in a high-entropy-alloy coating through increased lattice disorder and tangential force.
Prolonged extreme thermal cycling may degrade the nanolayered tribolayer.
Severe oxidation may chemically alter the engineered interface and limit its performance.
